inline.s: Dharma-medicine: the Buddha-Dharma is like medicine, able to cure the afflictions, suffering, and karmic hindrances of all sentient beings. Healing the three sufferings: healing sentient beings amid the three sufferings:
“Those not yet delivered, cause them to be delivered; those already delivered, cause them to attain Buddhahood.”

Sentient beings: also called living beings, that is, all creatures possessed of consciousness and feeling. The three sufferings: first, the suffering of suffering, the suffering produced by such painful conditions as cold and heat, hunger and thirst; second, the suffering of decay, the suffering produced when pleasant circumstances decay; third, the suffering of conditioning, the suffering of all conditioned dharmas’ impermanence and constant movement. To be raised to the rank of consecration and given the bodhi-prediction: this is
“those already delivered, cause them to attain Buddhahood”

: the Buddha’s hand is laid upon their crown and the prediction is given — at what time, in what land, and as what Buddha. (Please note: in this passage the sixteen great bodhisattvas have already become Buddhas and are turning the Dharma-wheel and delivering sentient beings; therefore “to be raised to the rank of consecration and given the bodhi-prediction” does not mean that they are being consecrated, but rather that this is what they do while delivering sentient beings.) Ācārya: also called ācārya, a teaching master.

In all Buddha-lands they are able to appear. Like a skilled illusionist who manifests various strange forms, yet within those forms nothing whatsoever is obtainable — these bodhisattvas are likewise so.

These sixteen great bodhisattvas, in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, are all able to manifest the eight marks of attaining the Way. Like a master illusionist who conjures up all manner of strange forms, yet within those forms there is in truth nothing whatsoever (this is said with respect to the true mark of all dharmas).
Buddha-land: a Buddha realm, a Buddha country — the land in which a Buddha dwells.

They penetrate the nature of all dharmas and comprehend the marks of sentient beings. They make offerings to all Buddhas and guide the multitudes of beings. Manifesting their bodies like flashes of lightning, they rend the net of Māra’s views and untie all bonds. They cause beings to rise far beyond the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and to enter the Dharma-gates of emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness. Skillfully establishing expedient means, they reveal the Three Vehicles.

These sixteen Buddhas who manifested the eight marks of attaining the Way penetrate the Dharma-nature and clearly comprehend the marks of sentient beings, clinging to neither of the two extremes of existence and nonexistence. They make offerings to all Buddhas and guide sentient beings. They manifest their bodies like lightning that lights up the earth on a pitch-black night, rending the net of Māra’s views and freeing sentient beings from the bonds of all deluded thinking and affliction. Teaching the One-Vehicle Dharma, they cause beings to rise far beyond the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and to enter the three gates of liberation — emptiness, wishlessness, and marklessness. For those beings who cannot yet accept the One-Vehicle Dharma, they skillfully establish expedient means and set forth the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Dharma-nature: the essential nature (the intrinsic substance) of all dharmas, another name for the true mark of all dharmas. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Sentient beings and Buddha-lands share one Dharma-nature.”
The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:
“The Dharma-nature, as was said above, is that each dharma is empty and all are one emptiness; this is the Dharma-nature.”

The two extremes of existence and nonexistence: clinging to the extreme of existence and clinging to the extreme of nonexistence are both wrong views. The three gates of liberation: three gates of wisdom that enter the state of liberation — first, the gate of emptiness, comprehending that all dharmas are originally empty without clinging to emptiness; second, the gate of wishlessness, knowing that all dharmas are illusory existents and therefore seeking nothing; third, the gate of marklessness, knowing that all dharmas are without marks and yet not without marks, thus entering the Middle Way. The One Vehicle: also called the One Buddha Vehicle, the sole teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. The Three Vehicles: the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle.
The passage below explains the last of the eight marks of attaining the Way: entering nirvāṇa (entering cessation, passing into extinction).
entering nirvāṇa
] The Buddha’s response-body takes its leave of the world (passes away).

The three bodies: the Dharma-body, the reward-body, and the response-body. First, the Dharma-body, also called the self-nature body or the Dharma-nature body — the true nature, unborn and undying, inherent in everyone; only we sentient beings are deluded and do not reveal it, while the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. Second, the reward-body, formed of the Buddha’s wisdom and merit; it has the distinction of the reward-body for self-enjoyment and the reward-body for others’ enjoyment — the reward-body for self-enjoyment is the body of inward realization and Dharma-bliss that the Buddha himself enjoys, while the reward-body for others’ enjoyment is the body manifested to teach the Dharma to bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. Third, the response-body, also called the transformation-body — the Buddha-body manifested in response to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings. Among these: the Dharma-body is ever-abiding; the reward-body has a beginning but no end; the response-body is manifested and has both birth and death.

For the sake of the middling and lesser, they manifest extinction. They attain all samādhis of non-birth and non-death, and gain all dhāraṇī-gates. At all times they awaken and enter the Avataṃsaka samādhi, fully possessing the dhāraṇīs and a hundred thousand samādhis. Dwelling in profound meditative concentration, they behold all Buddhas without exception, and in the space of a single thought travel throughout all Buddha-lands.

After these sixteen Buddhas who manifested the eight marks of attaining the Way had turned the great Dharma-wheel, they manifested the mark of entering cessation in order to benefit those of middling and lesser faculties. They realized the various samādhis of non-birth and non-death, and all the dhāraṇī-gates. At all times they awaken and enter the Avataṃsaka samādhi, fully possessing the dhāraṇīs and a hundred thousand samādhis. Dwelling in profound meditative concentration, they behold with their own eyes immeasurable Buddhas, and in a single thought travel throughout all Buddha-lands.
For the sake of the middling and lesser, they manifest extinction: manifesting the mark of entering cessation in order to benefit those of middling and lesser faculties. The Lotus Sutra
Chapter on the Measure of Life, says:

“If the Buddha were to remain long in the world, people of scant virtue, planting no roots of goodness, poor and lowly, greedy for the five desires, would enter the net of deluded recollection and false views. Seeing the Tathāgata ever present and never passing into extinction, they would grow arrogant and self-indulgent and harbor weariness and sloth, unable to give rise to the thought of how hard it is to meet a Buddha, or to a heart of reverence.
Therefore, though the Tathāgata does not in truth pass into extinction, he manifests extinction.”

Not extinguished yet manifesting extinction, and therefore called a “manifestation.” He makes this manifestation for the sake of delivering those of middling and lesser faculties. As for people of superior faculties who have awakened to the true mark of all dharmas, they see that the Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, is originally apart from birth and death — where could there be an extinction? Samādhi: also written sanmei, the dwelling of the mind on a single object without distraction or torpor. “They attain all samādhis of non-birth and non-death”: they attain the various samādhis of what is originally without birth or death (dharmas being originally unborn, they are therefore without death). The passage above, immediately after “and manifest extinction,” goes on to say “they attain all samādhis of non-birth and non-death,” showing that the Buddha’s entry into cessation is a manifestation of impermanence for the sake of delivering those of middling and lesser faculties. Though he manifests the mark of extinction (nirvāṇa), in reality he is the unborn, undying, equal, and ever-abiding thusness Dharma-body.

Dhāraṇī: rendered in Chinese as zongchi, “total retention” — that is, retaining all dharmas, so that good dharmas are not lost and evil dharmas do not arise. Avataṃsaka samādhi: also called Avataṃsaka concentration. This samādhi is the great samādhi that encompasses the whole Dharma-realm and enters all Buddha-Dharmas.

The above has told how these sixteen great bodhisattvas will go to the worlds of the ten directions to manifest the eight marks of attaining the Way: descending from Tuṣita (coming down from the Inner Court of the Tuṣita Heaven), entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing Māra, attaining Buddhahood, turning the Dharma-wheel, and entering nirvāṇa (entering cessation, passing into extinction).
The next two passages describe the present virtues of these sixteen great bodhisattvas.

Now these great beings have obtained the Buddha’s eloquence and abide in the practice of Samantabhadra. They are skilled at distinguishing the languages of sentient beings, opening and revealing the ultimate (the realm of reality), and they transcend all dharmas of the world. Their minds ever truly abide in the way of delivering the world; toward all things they are freely at ease, and for all classes of beings they are a friend who waits not to be asked. They receive and uphold the Tathāgata’s profound Dharma-treasury, and guard the Buddha’s lineage so that it is never cut off.

Now these sixteen great bodhisattvas have obtained the Buddha’s skill in expounding the meaning of the Dharma and abide in the great practice of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. They are skilled at distinguishing the languages of sentient beings and at guiding and teaching the One-Vehicle Dharma (opening and revealing the realm of reality). They transcend all dharmas of the world, grasping no marks, unmoved in thusness. Their minds ever truly abide in the way of delivering the world, and toward all things they are freely at ease (unentangled and unbound by anything). For all sentient beings they are a friend who waits not to be asked. They uphold the Tathāgata-garbha and cause the original nature ever to be present.

Abiding in the practice of Samantabhadra: the passage above has already said of these great beings that “they all alike cultivate the virtues of the great being Samantabhadra”; the present text says “abiding in the practice of Samantabhadra,” showing that all these great beings abide in the great practice of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. Opening and revealing the realm of reality: guiding and teaching the ultimate Dharma, that is, the One-Vehicle Dharma. The Lotus Sutra
Chapter Two, Expedient Means, says:
“The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to sentient beings solely by means of the One Buddha Vehicle
(the One-Vehicle Dharma)
; there is no other vehicle, neither two nor three.”

All classes of beings: all sentient beings. A friend who waits not to be asked: a true friend does not wait for an invitation, just as a loving mother instinctively protects her infant. To receive and uphold: to receive into the mind and practice as taught. The Tathāgata’s profound Dharma-treasury: that is, the Tathāgata-garbha. The Buddha’s lineage: that is, the original nature.

They rouse great compassion and pity sentient beings; they expound the eloquence of kindness and bestow the Dharma-eye; they close off the evil destinies and open the gate of goodness. Toward all sentient beings they look as upon themselves, rescuing them and bearing them up, ferrying them all across to the other shore. They all obtain the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas — wisdom, sagely clarity, inconceivable.

They rouse a heart of great compassion, pity sentient beings, lovingly expound the Dharma, and cause beings to gain right knowledge and right view (bestowing the Dharma-eye). They close off the evil destinies and throw wide the gate of goodness. They look upon all sentient beings as themselves, rescuing them and bearing them up, delivering them to the other shore of nirvāṇa. These sixteen great bodhisattvas all obtain the immeasurable merits of the Buddhas — wisdom, sagely clarity, inconceivable.

Evil destinies: synonymous with the evil paths. The gate of goodness: the gate by which one ends birth and death and realizes bodhi. “They all obtain the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas — wisdom, sagely clarity”: this shows that these sixteen great bodhisattvas are all bodhisattvas of equal enlightenment, and that their merit and wisdom are therefore nearly equal to a Buddha’s. Equal enlightenment: the fifty-first of the fifty-two stages of the Mahāyāna, called equal enlightenment — bodhisattvas who have fulfilled the ten grounds and are about to realize the Buddha-fruit, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to a Buddha’s, and who are therefore called “equal enlightenment”; also called “one life remaining in the succession,” because when this one life (the one life of transformation birth-and-death) is spent, they will succeed to the Buddha’s position.

Rousing great compassion, pitying sentient beings, expounding the eloquence of kindness, bestowing the Dharma-eye, closing off the evil destinies, opening the gate of goodness; toward all sentient beings looking as upon oneself, rescuing and bearing them up, ferrying them all across to the other shore” — this passage reveals the virtue of these sixteen great bodhisattvas’ unconditioned great loving-kindness and one-body great compassion.

Unconditioned great loving-kindness: though all Buddhas give joy and happiness to all sentient beings, they are apart from all discriminations of grasping and rejecting, and their minds take no object — this is called unconditioned great loving-kindness. One-body great compassion: all Buddhas truly know that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are three and yet without difference, and that the thusness Dharma-body is ultimately equal; on this ground they rouse a heart of great compassion to rescue and pull beings up — this is called one-body great compassion.
Great bodhisattvas such as these, immeasurable and boundless, gathered together at one time.
Great bodhisattvas such as these, immeasurable and boundless, all came together at the same time to attend the Dharma assembly.

There were also five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seven thousand pure-faith laymen, five hundred pure-faith laywomen, and the heavenly and Brahma multitudes of the Desire Realm and the Form Realm — all gathered in one great assembly.

There were also five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seven thousand pure-faith laymen, five hundred pure-faith laywomen, and the Brahma multitudes of the gods of the Desire Realm and the Form Realm, who likewise came to attend the Dharma assembly.

Bhikṣuṇī: a woman who has left home and received full ordination. Pure-faith layman: a man who has received the three refuges and the five precepts and possesses pure faith, called in Sanskrit upāsaka. Pure-faith laywoman: a woman who has received the three refuges and the five precepts and possesses pure faith, called in Sanskrit upāsikā. Brahma multitudes: the great assembly that cultivates the brahma-faring. Brahma-faring: pure conduct, namely the conduct of cutting off sexual desire.

blocks.text: 3. The Causal Origin of the Great Teaching

inline.s: At that time the World-Honored One’s majestic light blazed forth, like molten gold gathered into one, and again like a bright mirror whose reflections pervade within and without, manifesting a great radiance in many hundreds of thousands of transformations.

At that time the World-Honored One (Śākyamuni Buddha), by the brilliance of his majestic virtue, blazed resplendent like molten gold gathered into one, and again like a crystal-bright mirror whose light and reflections pervade within and without, brilliantly manifesting a great radiance whose forms and colors shifted and changed unceasingly in many hundreds of thousands of ways.
World-Honored One: an honorific title of the Buddha, because the Buddha is one honored by all the world.

This is the World-Honored One, about to expound the supreme and subtle Pure Land Dharma-gate, manifesting auspicious light in a manner most wondrous and peerless, in order to prompt Ānanda’s question and to cause those who hear to give rise to the thought of what is rare and hard to encounter, and so to practice as taught and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.

Manifesting auspicious light in a manner most wondrous and peerless: before expounding the perfect and sudden sutras, the World-Honored One would always manifest auspicious light. But the auspicious light manifested at this Dharma assembly was such as Venerable Ānanda had never seen in all the time he had attended the Buddha — this shows that the Sutra of Immeasurable Life is an extremely perfect and sudden, incomparably excellent sutra, the most rare of all.

Venerable Ānanda then reflected: today the World-Honored One’s physical body and all its faculties are joyful and pure; his radiant countenance is majestic, and jewel-lands appear in adornment. Never in all the time he had attended the Buddha had he seen such a sight. Rejoicing that he could now behold it, he gave rise to a heart of rare resolve.

Venerable Ānanda then reflected: today the World-Honored One’s physical body and faculties are joyful and pure, his radiant countenance majestic, and within the Buddha-light appear the jewel-adorned Buddha-lands of many kinds. Such a sight he had never seen in all the time he had attended the Buddha. Rejoicing that he could today behold it, he gave rise to a heart of rare and hard-to-encounter resolve.
The faculties: the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Joyful: glad and happy.
Majestic: the appearance of loftiness and supreme dignity.

Then he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt long with joined palms, and addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, today you have entered the great serene concentration and abide in the wondrous Dharma, in the guide’s practice and the supreme way in which all Buddhas abide. Past, future, and present — Buddha recollects Buddha. Are you now recollecting the Buddhas of past and future, or the Buddhas of the present in other directions? Why is your majestic power so resplendent, your light and auspicious signs so wondrous and peerless? Pray reveal it to us.

Thereupon he rose at once from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt long with joined palms, and addressed the Buddha: World-Honored One, today you have entered the great serene concentration and abide in the wondrous Dharma, abiding in the guide’s practice and the supreme way in which all Buddhas abide. The Buddhas of past, future, and present — Buddha recollects Buddha. Is the World-Honored One now recollecting the Buddhas of past and future, or the Buddhas of the present in other directions? Why is your majestic power so resplendent, your light and auspicious signs so wondrous and peerless, even to such a degree? Pray expound it for the great assembly.

Baring (tǎn) the right shoulder: leaving the right shoulder bare, abbreviated as “baring the shoulder” — that is, when wearing the kāṣāya, to bare the right shoulder and cover the left, a ceremonial form expressing respect. To address [the Buddha]: for a junior to speak respectfully to a senior, or a subordinate to a superior. Majestic power: majestic virtue and spiritual powers.
Thereupon the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: Excellent! Excellent! For the sake of compassion and benefit for all sentient beings, you have been able to ask about so subtle a meaning. This
(that is, this)

question of yours surpasses by a hundred thousand million times the merit of making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of a whole world, and of giving gifts for many kalpas to the gods and people of the heavens and to creatures that fly and crawl. Why is that? Because the gods and people of the future and all sentient beings will, through your question, attain deliverance.

Thereupon the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: Well asked! Well asked! For the sake of compassion and benefit for all sentient beings, you have been able to ask about so subtle a meaning. This question of yours today surpasses by a hundred thousand million times the merit of making offerings to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of a whole world, and of giving gifts for many kalpas to the gods and people of the heavens and even to insects (creatures that fly and crawl). Why is that? Because the gods and people of the future, and all sentient beings, will all attain deliverance through this one question of yours.
This question of yours ... the gods and people of the future and all sentient beings will all attain deliverance through your question” — this passage shows the vast merit of Ānanda’s question.
Excellent! Excellent! Well asked! Well asked! The World-Honored One was greatly delighted by Ānanda’s question and praised him highly.
Pratyekabuddha: one who awakens to the Way by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination and realizing the principle of true emptiness.
Flying (
xuān

) insects: insects that can fly. Crawling (rú) creatures: insects that crawl. Beings possessed of spirit: animals endowed with consciousness. “All will attain deliverance through your question”: had Ānanda not asked and the World-Honored One not revealed the Pure Land Dharma-gate, then for sentient beings to end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth, they would have to cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought) — and in the age of the Final Dharma scarcely one in a hundred million succeeds.
Yet in cultivating the Pure Land Dharma-gate, if only the method is correct and one strives with diligence, then of ten thousand who cultivate, ten thousand will go!
Ānanda, the Tathāgata, out of inexhaustible great compassion, in pity for
jīn

the three realms, has appeared in the world. Gloriously he unfolds the teaching of the Way, wishing to rescue the multitudes of beings and bestow upon them the true benefit. He is hard to meet and hard to see, like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing. Your question today brings benefit to many.

Ānanda, the Tathāgata, out of inexhaustible great compassion, pities the sentient beings of the three realms, and therefore appears in the world. Gloriously he unfolds the teaching of the great Way, in order to rescue the multitudes of beings throughout the world and to bestow upon them the true benefit. The Tathāgata’s appearing in the world is hard to meet and hard to see, like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing. Your question today greatly benefits sentient beings.
Tathāgata: the Buddha rides the way of thusness and comes to the three realms to teach, and is therefore called “Tathāgata.” Jīn’āi (jin, pitying): to feel compassion. The multitudes of beings (
méng

): the populace, the common people. Méng is interchangeable with méng (the common folk); here “the multitudes of common folk” means sentient beings. “Like the udumbara flower, rarely appearing”: the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra says:
“The udumbara flower — this means the auspicious omen, appearing once in three thousand years.”

To benefit: to cause others to receive advantage. “Your question today brings benefit to many”: Ānanda’s question today has caused the Pure Land Dharma-gate to shine forth in the world — our gratitude is endless!

Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One, has wisdom that cannot be measured and is without any obstruction. He can, in the space of a single thought, abide in the world for immeasurable millions of kalpas, while his body and faculties neither increase nor decrease. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are utterly unimpeded and without limit, and because he has attained the supreme mastery over all dharmas.

Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One, has wisdom that cannot be measured and knows no obstruction. He can, in the space of a single thought, abide in the world for immeasurable millions of kalpas, while the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind and all his other faculties neither increase nor decrease in the least. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are utterly unhindered and inexhaustible, and because he has attained the supreme mastery over all dharmas.

Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened: also called equal and perfect enlightenment, one of the Tathāgata’s ten honored titles. “Abiding in the world for immeasurable millions of kalpas”: the Assembly of the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Life (the Tang translation) says:
“Ānanda, the Tathāgata, the Worthy
(the Worthy One, the arhat)

, the Perfectly Enlightened One, if he wishes to abide in the world, can in the time of a single meal abide for immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas. And if he should increase that number beyond the above, the Tathāgata’s body and faculties would neither increase nor decrease.”
The Worthy One: one of the Tathāgata’s ten honored titles.

The Tathāgata’s ten titles: the Tathāgata has ten honored titles. 1. The Worthy One (arhat): worthy to receive the offerings of gods and humans. 2. Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened: truly and universally knowing all dharmas. 3. Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct: fully possessing the three insights — the insight of past lives, the heavenly eye, and the extinction of outflows — together with the five practices of the noble, the brahma-faring, the heavenly, the infant, and the sick. 4. Well-Gone: freely and well departed, having entered nirvāṇa. 5. Knower of the World: able to understand the affairs and principles of all worlds. 6. Supreme One: the one who is loftiest of all. 7. Tamer of Men: able to train and guide the great men who cultivate the right path. 8. Teacher of Gods and Humans: the Buddha is the guide of all gods and humans. 9. Buddha: the abbreviation of the Sanskrit “buddha,” rendered in Chinese as “the Awakened One” — the great sage who has awakened to the truth of the universe and of human life. 10. World-Honored One: the one honored in common by all the world.
Ānanda, listen attentively and ponder it well; I will now explain it to you in detail.
Ānanda, you must listen carefully, receive it and savor it well; I will explain it to you point by point.

blocks.text: Part Two: The Main Body Section

inline.s: The Main Body Section is the principal part of this piece, running from the fourth chapter through the forty-second. It is divided into four units in all: 1. attaining Buddhahood and establishing the Buddha-land; 2. the dependent and direct rewards of the Land of Utmost Bliss; 3. the practice and realization of rebirth there; 4. joyfully seeking and wearily renouncing.

blocks.text: 1. Attaining Buddhahood and Establishing the Buddha-Land

inline.s: Establishing the Buddha-land: founding a Buddha-country:
“May I abide in samādhi, ever sending forth light to illumine all, and thereby attain a vast and pure abode, supremely adorned beyond all compare.”
Bhikṣu Dharmākara: Dharmākara is the name of Amitabha Buddha in the causal ground.

The Buddha told Ānanda: In ages past, immeasurably long ago, throughout inconceivable, countless kalpas, there was a Tathāgata named Blossoming Light who appeared in the world, teaching and delivering immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the Way, and then entering cessation. After him there was a Tathāgata named Far-Reaching Light; next named Moonlight; next named Sandalwood Fragrance; next named King of Goodly Mountains; next named Sumeru Heaven-Crown; next named Sumeru Equal Radiance; next named Moon-Hued; next named Right Mindfulness; next named Free of Defilement; next named Non-Attachment; next named Dragon Heaven; next named Night Light; next named Peaceful Radiant Summit; next named Immovable Ground; next named Wondrous Vaiḍūrya Flower; next named Vaiḍūrya Golden Hue; next named Golden Treasury; next named Flaming Light; next named Flaming Root; next named Earth-Seed; next named Moon Image; next named Sun Sound; next named Flower of Liberation; next named Adorned Radiance; next named Ocean-Awakening Spiritual Power; next named Water Light; next named Great Fragrance; next named Free of Dust and Defilement; next named Abandoning Weary Thought; next named Jewel Flame; next named Wondrous Summit; next named Courageously Established; next named Merit-Upholding Wisdom; next named Hiding Sun and Moon Light; next named Sun-and-Moon Vaiḍūrya Light; next named Supreme Vaiḍūrya Light; next named Highest Head; next named Bodhi Flower; next named Moon Brightness; next named Sunlight; next named King of Flower Hue; next named Water-Moon Light; next named Dispelling Delusion’s Darkness; next named Crossing the Veil of Conduct; next named Pure Faith; next named Good Dwelling; next named Majestic Spirit; next named Dharma Wisdom; next named Phoenix Sound; next named Lion Sound; next named Dragon Sound; next named Dwelling in the World — all such Buddhas have already passed away.

The Buddha said to Ānanda: Throughout the inconceivable, countless kalpas of the immeasurably distant past, there was a Blossoming Light Tathāgata who appeared in the world, teaching and delivering immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the Way, and then manifesting cessation. After him there was a Tathāgata named Far-Reaching Light, then Moonlight, then Sandalwood Fragrance, then King of Goodly Mountains, then Sumeru Heaven-Crown, then Sumeru Equal Radiance, then Moon-Hued, then Right Mindfulness, then Free of Defilement, then Non-Attachment, then Dragon Heaven, then Night Light, then Peaceful Radiant Summit, then Immovable Ground, then Wondrous Vaiḍūrya Flower, then Vaiḍūrya Golden Hue, then Golden Treasury, then Flaming Light, then Flaming Root, then Earth-Seed, then Moon Image, then Sun Sound, then Flower of Liberation, then Adorned Radiance, then Ocean-Awakening Spiritual Power, then Water Light, then Great Fragrance, then Free of Dust and Defilement, then Abandoning Weary Thought, then Jewel Flame, then Wondrous Summit, then Courageously Established, then Merit-Upholding Wisdom, then Hiding Sun and Moon Light, then Sun-and-Moon Vaiḍūrya Light, then Supreme Vaiḍūrya Light, then Highest Head, then Bodhi Flower, then Moon Brightness, then Sunlight, then King of Flower Hue, then Water-Moon Light, then Dispelling Delusion’s Darkness, then Crossing the Veil of Conduct, then Pure Faith, then Good Dwelling, then Majestic Spirit, then Dharma Wisdom, then Phoenix Sound, then Lion Sound, then Dragon Sound, then Dwelling in the World. All such Buddhas have already passed away.

At that time there next appeared a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja, the Tathāgata — the Worthy One, the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Supreme One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He taught in the world for forty-two kalpas, constantly expounding the sutras and the Way to the gods and to the people of the world.
At that time,

there appeared another Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata — the Worthy One, the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Supreme One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He taught sentient beings in the world for fully forty-two kalpas, constantly expounding the sutras and the Way to the gods and to the people of the world.
Boundless: without limit or end, describing an extremely long time.

There was a great king of a country named World-Rich King who, hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, rejoiced and understood, and thereupon brought forth the unsurpassed, true intention of the Way. He abandoned his kingdom and gave up his throne, became a śramaṇa, and was known as Dharmākara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.

At that time there was a king of a great country named World-Rich King. Hearing the Buddha teach the Dharma, he gave rise to great joy, suddenly awakened, and thereupon brought forth the unsurpassed, true intention of the Way. He then abandoned the throne, shaved his head, and left home, and was known as Dharmākara, cultivating the bodhisattva path.
World-Rich King: the Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment as Spoken by the Buddha (the Han translation) says:

“The Buddha taught the sutras and the Way to the gods and to the people of the world, and none could surpass him. World-Rich King, hearing the sutras and the Way, rejoiced and understood, and thereupon abandoned his kingdom and became a bhikṣu.”

Seeking: in a moment. Śramaṇa: the general term for one who has left home to cultivate the Way. The bodhisattva path: that is, the six pāramitās — the path by which one perfects benefit for self and others and attains the Buddha-fruit. The six pāramitās: the six dharmas by which one may cross from this shore of birth-and-death and affliction to the other shore of nirvāṇa’s peace and bliss — giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and prajñā. Giving overcomes stinginess and greed; precepts overcome transgression; patience overcomes anger; vigor overcomes laziness; concentration overcomes distraction; prajñā overcomes delusion. The details are as in the table below:

Of lofty ability, brave and wise, he transcended and differed from the world; in faith, understanding, clarity, and memory he was foremost in all. He also had supreme vows of practice, together with the powers of mindfulness and wisdom, which enhanced his mind so that it was firm and unmoved. In cultivation and vigor, none could surpass him.

Bhikṣu Dharmākara’s abilities were extraordinary; brave and vigorous, wise and clear-minded, he far surpassed all people in the world. In receiving the teachings with faith, in understanding, in clarity of principle, and in memory, he was foremost in all. He also had supreme vows and aspirations, together with the five powers of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, by which he enhanced his mind, so that before hardship, peril, intimidation, and enticement he stood firm and unmoved. In cultivation and vigor, none could surpass him.

The power of mindfulness and wisdom: here mindfulness and wisdom stand for the five powers. The five powers: the power of faith, the power of vigor, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, able to destroy all wrong faiths; the power of vigor is the growth of the root of vigor, able to destroy the body’s laziness; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, able to destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the root of concentration, able to destroy all deluded imaginings; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, able to destroy all the delusions of the three realms (the Desire Realm, the Form Realm, and the Formless Realm).
He went to where the Buddha was, bowed in homage, knelt long, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and thereupon praised the Buddha in gāthā and brought forth vast vows.
He came to the dwelling place of Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, bowed in homage, knelt long, joined his palms toward the Buddha, praised the Buddha in verse, and brought forth vast vows.
Gāthā: rendered in Chinese as “verse.”
The verse says:

The Tathāgata’s form is wondrous-fair,
in all the world no equal is there.

His light is measureless, illumining the ten directions wide;
the sun, the moon, fire, and jewels all hide
yào, bright
Sun, moon, fire, and jewels all hide their brightness: the light of the sun, the moon, fire, and precious jewels is altogether hidden and unseen.

The World-Honored One sounds but one single note;
each sentient being hears it as befits his lot.

And one wondrous form he can display,
that all beings may see each in his own way.

The World-Honored One can expound with a single sound, yet beings of every kind hear their own language and all understand the principle he sets forth. He can also manifest one subtle form, so that beings of every kind all see the very bodily form of their own kind that pleases them most.

May I attain the Buddha’s voice, pure and clear,
my Dharma-sound reaching all lands far and near.

Proclaiming the gates of precepts, samādhi, and zeal,
and penetrating the Dharma profound, subtle, and real.

Precepts and concentration: this is the abbreviated form of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Precepts, concentration, and wisdom: also called the three trainings, or the three trainings without outflows. Precepts means to stop evil conduct by precepts; concentration means to fix the mind upon one place; wisdom means to break through delusion and realize the truth. Precepts can subdue the mind of greed and craving; concentration can subdue the mind of anger; wisdom can subdue the mind of deluded ignorance. Upholding these three dharmas of precepts, concentration, and wisdom can counteract the three poisons and accomplish the Buddha-fruit; therefore they are called the “three trainings without outflows.”

His wisdom is vast and deep as the sea,
his mind pure within, from affliction free.

He passes beyond the boundless gates of evil fate,
and swiftly reaches the ultimate shore of bodhi, perfect and great.
Free of the dust of toil: without affliction. “Dust of toil” is another name for affliction. The ultimate shore of bodhi: the perfection of Buddhahood.

Ignorance, greed, and anger forever gone,
delusion ended, faults extinguished — by samādhi’s power alone.

And like the immeasurable Buddhas of the past,
for those multitudes a great guiding master, first and last.

“Ignorance, greed, and anger forever gone; delusion ended, faults extinguished — by the power of samādhi”: by the power of samādhi, cutting off forever the greed, anger, and delusion of ignorance, together with the delusions of view and thought, and every fault.

He can rescue every world beneath the sky,
from birth, age, sickness, death, and sorrow’s cry.

Ever practicing giving, precepts, patience, zeal,
vigor, concentration, wisdom — the six pāramitās’ wheel.
The six pāramitās: that is, the six pāramitās, also known as the six crossings.

Those not yet saved, may they be saved and carried o’er;
those saved, may they attain to Buddhahood forevermore.

Though one made offerings to sages countless as the Ganges’ sand,
it were not equal to firm courage seeking the enlightenment-land.

“Those not yet saved, cause them to be saved; those already saved, cause them to attain Buddhahood”: sentient beings who have not yet ended fragmentary birth-and-death are caused to end fragmentary birth-and-death, and sentient beings who have already ended fragmentary birth-and-death are caused to end transformation birth-and-death and attain Buddhahood. Fragmentary birth-and-death: sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, whose lifespans are all limited and whose bodies are all segmented, owing to the retribution of good and evil karma; hence their birth and death are called “fragmentary birth-and-death.” One who has ended fragmentary birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. Cutting off the delusions of view and thought is to end fragmentary birth-and-death — an arhat, for example. Transformation birth-and-death: the sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended fragmentary birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the Way, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each period of this shifting of delusion and awakening differs, and the passage from the earlier period into the later is just like one birth and death, and is therefore called “transformation birth-and-death.” One who has ended transformation birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit. “Though one made offerings to sages countless as the Ganges’ sand, it is not equal to firm courage in seeking perfect enlightenment”: though one made offerings to as many Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, it would still not equal one’s own resolute and courageous seeking of the way to Buddhahood, because in this way one can deliver sentient beings all the more. Ganges sand: the Ganges is a great river of India, and its waters hold much fine sand; when the Buddha taught the Dharma, he often used the number of fine sand grains in the Ganges to describe an extremely great number.

May I abide in samādhi’s steady light,
and ever shine my radiance on all, by day and night.

And thus attain a pure abode, vast and fair,
supremely adorned, with nothing to compare.

The vast and pure abode: the pure Buddha-land evoked and manifested when Bhikṣu Dharmākara attained Buddhahood — the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. “Attaining a vast and pure abode”: a Buddha-land is evoked and manifested by a Buddha’s perfect merit, blessing, and wisdom. Beyond all compare: there is nothing that can be compared with it.

All you beings who through the destinies roam,
come swiftly to my land and find peace at home.

Ever with a loving mind I’ll rescue those in distress,
and ferry all the boundless suffering hosts to blessedness.
Pulling beings up: drawing out the suffering of sentient beings.

My resolve is firm, my strength of vow is sure;
only a Buddha’s sage wisdom can know it pure.

Even should this body dwell amid all woe,
this vow-heart of mine shall never backward go.
Gathering in the Buddha-land: to design it concretely and draw up the “blueprint” of the Buddha-land.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha: I am now cultivating the bodhisattva path and have already brought forth the unsurpassed heart of perfect enlightenment; I vow to become a Buddha, altogether like the Buddha. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the sutras and Dharma for me; I shall receive and uphold them, practice as taught, uproot the root of birth and death with all its toil and suffering, and swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

When Bhikṣu Dharmākara had finished speaking this verse, he addressed the Buddha: I now walk the bodhisattva path and have already brought forth the heart of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, vowing to become a Buddha, in all things like the Buddha. May the Buddha broadly proclaim the sutras and Dharma for me; I shall receive and uphold them, practice as taught, uproot the root of birth and death with all its toil and suffering, and swiftly realize the Buddha-fruit (swiftly attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment).

When I attain Buddhahood, may my wisdom and radiance, the land I dwell in, and the name of its teaching lord be heard throughout the ten directions. May the gods and people, and creatures that fly and crawl, who come to be born in my land, all become bodhisattvas. If I establish these vows and they surpass those of countless Buddha-lands — can this be attained?

When I attain Buddhahood, may my wisdom and radiance, the Buddha-land I establish (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss), and the name of its teaching lord (Amitabha Buddha) be heard throughout the ten directions. May the gods and people, and even creatures that fly and crawl, who come to be born in my land, all become bodhisattvas. If I establish these vows and they all surpass those of countless Buddha-lands, can this be attained?
Teaching lord
] The Buddha is the lord of the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system that he teaches and transforms.

The name of the teaching lord: that is, the name under which Bhikṣu Dharmākara will become a Buddha (Amitabha Buddha). The land he establishes: that is, the Buddha-land established when Dharmākara becomes a Buddha (the Western Land of Utmost Bliss).

Lokeśvararāja Buddha then spoke these sutra words for Dharmākara: Suppose a man were to measure the great ocean with a bushel, and after passing through kalpas he could still reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart and does not cease his vigor, he will surely achieve the fruit — what vow could he fail to attain?

Lokeśvararāja Buddha then spoke these sutra words for Dharmākara: Suppose a man were to measure the great ocean with a bushel; after passing through many kalpas he could still reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart and does not cease his vigor, he will surely succeed — what vow could he fail to accomplish?
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life as Spoken by the Buddha (the Wei translation) says:

“At that time Lokeśvararāja Buddha, knowing that he was lofty and wise, and that his vows were deep and vast, spoke these sutra words for Bhikṣu Dharmākara: Suppose a man were to measure the great ocean with a bushel, and after passing through kalpas he could still reach the bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures. If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart and unceasing vigor, he will surely achieve the fruit — what vow could he fail to attain?”

Sincere heart: a heart utterly sincere and firm. When such a heart is brought forth, the sage-fruit is necessarily contained within it; because the cause penetrates the ocean of fruition, flower and fruit are simultaneous — one need only be vigorous; what vow could fail to be attained?
Achieving the fruit (kèguǒ):
to succeed.

Reflect for yourself: by cultivating what expedient means can you accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land? As to how you should practice, you yourself should know. A pure Buddha-land you must gather in yourself.

Reflect for yourself: by cultivating what can you accomplish such an adorned Buddha-land? As to how you should practice, you yourself should know. A pure Buddha-land you should gather in yourself (design it concretely and draw up the “blueprint”).
Cultivating what expedient means: “expedient means” here refers to methods of practice. “Can accomplish the adornment of a Buddha-land”: that you may accomplish the adornment of your Buddha-land.

“You must gather it in yourself”: you should gather it in yourself (design it concretely and draw up the “blueprint”). A Buddha-land is evoked and manifested by a Buddha’s perfect merit, blessing, and wisdom; “Chapter Four, The Causal Ground of Dharmākara” says:
“Thus he attained a vast and pure abode, supremely adorned beyond all compare.”

And first of all, this vast and pure abode, supremely adorned beyond all compare, had to be concretely designed and its detailed “blueprint” drawn. For this, Bhikṣu Dharmākara spent fully five kalpas of time.

Dharmākara said: This meaning is vast and profound, beyond my realm. I only pray that the Tathāgata, the Worthy and Rightly Enlightened One, will broadly set forth the immeasurable wondrous Buddha-lands of all Buddhas. If I may hear such dharmas as these, ponder and cultivate them, I vow to fulfill all my vows.

Dharmākara said: This meaning is too profound; it exceeds my realm. I only pray that the Tathāgata will broadly set forth the immeasurable wondrous Buddha-lands of all Buddhas. If I may hear such dharmas as these, ponder and cultivate them, I vow to fulfill all my vows.

Tathāgata, the Worthy and Rightly Enlightened One: that is, Tathāgata, the Worthy One (arhat), and the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One. Among these, the Worthy One and the Rightly and Perfectly Enlightened One are the first and second of the Tathāgata’s ten titles.

Lokeśvararāja Buddha, knowing that he was lofty and wise, and that his vows were deep and vast, then proclaimed for him the marks of the meritorious adornment and purity, the vastness and perfection, of twenty-one billion Buddha-lands. In accordance with his heart’s wish, he manifested them all before him. While this Dharma was being taught, a thousand million years passed.
